```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A smooth describes a relationship without requiring it to be linear. glmmTMB
can estimate these relationships alongside its other model components, and
gratia can now extract and display their effects. The examples below ask how
annual river flow changes over time and how plants respond to increasing carbon
dioxide concentration. The second example also accounts for measurements on
the same plant.

This article needs the optional package glmmTMB, with support for `mgcv::s()`
terms; the examples were developed with glmmTMB 1.1.15.9000 and mgcv 1.9-4.
Smooth fitting remains experimental in glmmTMB. Its
[fitting documentation](https://glmmtmb.github.io/glmmTMB/reference/glmmTMB.html)
recommends `REML = TRUE`. Use an unqualified `s()` in the formula after attaching
mgcv, rather than replacing the smooth with an unpenalised spline basis.
The smoothing penalty is estimated during fitting.

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library("mgcv")
library("glmmTMB")
library("gratia")
library("ggplot2")
```

## How did the mean annual flow of the Nile change?

The [Nile data](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/Nile.html)
contain 100 annual flow measurements at Aswan from 1871 to 1970, measured in
units of $10^8$ cubic metres. The question here is descriptive: what broad
change in mean flow is supported by these observations? We adapt the smooth
example in the glmmTMB documentation, name the variables `year` and `flow`, and
fit the same spline with mgcv for comparison.

```{r nile-data}
nile <- data.frame(
  year = as.numeric(time(Nile)),
  flow = as.numeric(Nile)
)
ggplot(nile, aes(year, flow)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = expression(Annual ~ flow ~ (10^8 ~ m^3)))
```

Annual flow is continuous. A Gaussian model is a reasonable starting point for
departures around a smooth mean, provided its residual spread is reasonably
stable. The observations are a time series, so independence needs checking;
year appearing in a smooth does not itself model residual serial dependence.

```{r nile-fit}
nile_gam <- gam(flow ~ s(year, k = 10), data = nile, method = "REML")
nile_tmb <- glmmTMB(flow ~ s(year, k = 10), data = nile,
  family = gaussian(), REML = TRUE, start = list(theta = 5))
summary(nile_tmb)
```

`k = 10` sets the size of the available spline basis, rather than fixing ten
effective degrees of freedom. The fitted penalty discourages unnecessary
wiggliness. `start` follows the package's Nile example and supplies an initial
log standard deviation for the spline's random coefficients; it does not fix
their fitted variance. Inspect convergence and warnings when adapting this
example to other data. The `dummy` random effect in the printed summary is part
of the spline representation, not an additional sampled group.

## Extract the trend and read its uncertainty

```{r nile-extraction}
smooths(nile_tmb)
head(smooth_coefs(nile_tmb, select = "s(year)"))
trend <- smooth_estimates(nile_tmb, select = "s(year)",
  interval = "credible")
head(trend)
draw(trend, xlab = "Year", ylab = expression(Flow ~ contribution ~ (10^8 ~ m^3)))
```

The curve is the smooth's contribution relative to its centring constraint,
not the full expected flow. Positive values indicate flow above the fitted
intercept. The broad decline from the late nineteenth century to the early
twentieth century is much clearer than the small subsequent undulations.
The shaded region concerns uncertainty in the fitted mean contribution; it
does not describe the spread of individual annual observations.

The default interval uses the joint TMB covariance, transformed back to the
mgcv smooth coefficients. It includes covariance between fixed and fitted
random coefficients. This is not mgcv's frequentist covariance or its optional
correction for uncertainty in smoothing parameters: `frequentist = TRUE` and
`unconditional = TRUE` are unavailable for glmmTMB effects.

At any particular year a pointwise interval is useful. If the claim concerns
the entire plotted trend, ask for a simultaneous band instead:

```{r nile-simultaneous}
draw(nile_tmb, select = "s(year)", interval = "simultaneous",
  n = 120, n_sim = 3000, seed = 71,
  xlab = "Year", ylab = expression(Flow ~ contribution ~ (10^8 ~ m^3)))
```

The wider band has approximate coverage over the finite evaluation grid of
this smooth. It is not a prediction interval, and it does not claim joint
coverage across all model terms. `interval = "credible"` is an alias for the
pointwise `"confidence"` option. With mgcv models, `smooth_estimates()` also
allows `frequentist = TRUE`; that changes the covariance used, rather than
changing a pointwise statement into a simultaneous one. `get_vcov()` makes the
chosen model covariance available for custom calculations.

For the full expected flow, add the intercept. Here the model has just one
smooth and an identity link, so this gives a direct comparison with both
packages' predictions:

```{r nile-predictions}
year_grid <- data.frame(year = seq(1871, 1970, length.out = 120))
full_trend <- smooth_estimates(nile_tmb, data = year_grid,
  interval = "credible")
full_trend$mean_flow <- full_trend$.estimate + unname(fixef(nile_tmb)$cond[1])
full_trend$lower <- full_trend$.lower_ci + unname(fixef(nile_tmb)$cond[1])
full_trend$upper <- full_trend$.upper_ci + unname(fixef(nile_tmb)$cond[1])
full_trend$mgcv_mean <- as.numeric(predict(nile_gam, newdata = year_grid))
ggplot(full_trend, aes(year, mean_flow)) +
  geom_point(data = nile, aes(y = flow), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_line(aes(y = mgcv_mean), colour = "steelblue", linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = expression(Annual ~ flow ~ (10^8 ~ m^3)),
    subtitle = "glmmTMB mean and interval; dashed blue line is the mgcv mean")
```

`overall_uncertainty = TRUE`, the default, includes uncertainty in the model
constant in the smooth's standard errors. Adding the intercept to the displayed
values therefore gives appropriate mean intervals for this one-smooth model.
For a model with several terms, adding only the intercept would leave out the
other contributions; use predictions from the full model instead. The two
mean curves almost coincide here because the models use the same Gaussian
likelihood and spline penalty. Such agreement is not expected automatically
for non-Gaussian fits or more complex random-effect structures.

For the mgcv fit, we can compare the two covariance choices at years of
interest while leaving the estimated trend unchanged:

```{r nile-covariance-choices}
comparison_years <- data.frame(year = c(1880, 1920))
bayesian_effect <- smooth_estimates(nile_gam, data = comparison_years)
frequentist_effect <- smooth_estimates(nile_gam, data = comparison_years,
  frequentist = TRUE, interval = "confidence")
data.frame(year = comparison_years$year,
  contribution = bayesian_effect$.estimate,
  bayesian_se = bayesian_effect$.se,
  frequentist_se = frequentist_effect$.se)
gam_covariance <- get_vcov(nile_gam, frequentist = TRUE)
```

The frequentist covariance concerns sampling variability of the penalised
coefficient estimator with smoothing parameters held fixed. Smaller standard
errors do not account for the bias introduced by penalisation. The default
approximate Bayesian covariance is usually the useful starting point for
smooth-effect intervals; neither choice resolves residual serial dependence.
The final line extracts the chosen covariance for custom calculations.

## Does the fitted distribution explain variation around the trend?

```{r nile-checks}
appraise(nile_tmb, type = "pearson", method = "simulate",
  n_simulate = 100, seed = 72)
residual_correlation_plot(nile_tmb, type = "pearson", lag_max = 15)
```

The panel uses glmmTMB's native Pearson residuals. For this Gaussian fit they
remain on the scale of the flow response, rather than standard-normal scores.
Simulated QQ references hold the fitted smooth fixed and generate new
annual responses. They check the response distribution under this fitted
model; they do not refit the trend. The separate autocorrelation plot asks
whether successive departures still resemble one another. Its correlations
describe ordered residual structure, with no significance bands that assume
independent residuals. Lags are observation positions; here each position
corresponds to one year.

Most of the QQ points follow their simulated reference, with the lowest-flow
observation standing out in the lower tail. That does not establish a correct
model: the serial-correlation check asks a separate question.

The residual correlation at lag one is about 0.24, with much smaller correlation
at lag two. Some adjacent-year structure remains after removing the smooth
trend. This is a reason to consider a time-series model when the precision of
the trend or forecasts matters; it is not a significance test for independence.

The decline is supported as a description of this series. It does not identify
a cause, establish a precisely dated abrupt change, or make the fitted spline
a reliable forecasting model. A change-point or time-series analysis asks
different questions and may give different uncertainty. See
[Choosing diagnostic references](model-checking.html) for checks of
dependence and for the distinction between holding effects fixed, drawing
their uncertainty and simulating new effects.

## Do repeated measurements change how we read plant responses?

The `CO2` experiment recorded carbon dioxide uptake by twelve plants of
*Echinochloa crus-galli* at seven concentrations. Plants came from Quebec or
Mississippi and received chilled or nonchilled treatment. See `?datasets::CO2`
for the experiment and units. Uptake is positive, and a Gamma model with a log
link allows its residual variance to grow with the mean. Measurements from
one plant share individual characteristics. The 84 measurements provide only
twelve independently treated plants.

We use a shared smooth response to concentration, an origin-by-treatment
interaction, and plant-specific intercepts and slopes. These slopes allow
individual plants to differ in their response to concentration without
assuming that the population response itself is linear.

```{r plant-data-model}
plant <- as.data.frame(CO2)
plant$Plant <- factor(plant$Plant, ordered = FALSE)
plant$log_conc <- log(plant$conc) - mean(log(plant$conc))
plant_tmb <- glmmTMB(
  uptake ~ Type * Treatment + s(log_conc, k = 5) + (1 + log_conc | Plant),
  data = plant, family = Gamma(link = "log"), REML = TRUE)
summary(plant_tmb)
```

For non-Gaussian responses, glmmTMB also advises checking REML
behaviour with simulations for the intended design. The fitted example
demonstrates the workflow; it does not establish interval calibration for
another experiment.

The centred log concentration improves the interpretation of plant intercepts:
they apply at the geometric mean concentration. The shared curve represents
rapid change at low concentrations and slower change at high concentrations.
The treatment interaction allows its shift in log mean uptake to differ by
origin. With only three plants in each origin-treatment combination, the
treatment estimates remain uncertain.

```{r plant-effects, fig.height = 9}
draw(plant_tmb, ncol = 2)
```

`draw()` includes smooths, native random effects and parametric effects by
default. The Gaussian QQ panels for plant intercepts and slopes show fitted
plant deviations, not response residuals. The random coefficients that encode
the spline are excluded from these panels. `parametric = FALSE` omits
parametric panels; an explicit `select` draws only selected effects unless
`parametric = TRUE` is also supplied.

```{r plant-random-lines}
draw(plant_tmb, select = c("(1 | Plant)", "(log_conc | Plant)"),
  ranef_lines = TRUE)
```

These lines are each plant's random contribution $b_{0j} + x b_{1j}$ on the
log scale. They do not include the shared curve or treatment means and have
no uncertainty bands. This display requires a simple numeric intercept-slope
pair from the same formula term. Multiple slopes, transformed or factor slopes,
and structured covariance terms retain separate QQ panels.

The interaction deserves a focused view rather than interpreting two main
effects separately:

```{r plant-parametric-interaction}
parametric_terms(plant_tmb)
draw(parametric_effects(plant_tmb, terms = "Type:Treatment"))
```

These are contrast-coded partial contributions on the log scale. A zero
reference-category contribution is a coding convention. It is not evidence
that the reference plants have zero uptake. Parametric intervals now include
intercept uncertainty and its covariance with the term by default; use
`overall_uncertainty = FALSE` for uncertainty in the term alone. The estimated
partial contributions do not change. Full predictions combine all terms:

```{r plant-full-predictions}
plant$expected <- as.numeric(predict(plant_tmb, type = "response"))
ggplot(plant, aes(conc, uptake, group = Plant, colour = Treatment)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(y = expected)) +
  facet_wrap(~ Type) +
  labs(x = "Carbon dioxide concentration (mL/L)",
    y = expression(CO[2] ~ uptake ~ (mu * mol ~ m^{-2} ~ s^{-1})))
```

The curves describe these observed plants, including their fitted deviations.
They are not marginal mean curves for a new plant. The Gamma model and common
nonlinear shape are working assumptions that should be checked:

```{r plant-diagnostics}
appraise(plant_tmb, type = "quantile", seed = 73)
```

The lowest quantile score stands out below the normal reference: one
measurement is substantially lower than its fitted distribution would
typically produce. Inspect that observation and the fitted curve for its plant
before assuming the model explains every replicate equally well.
[Read smooth effects, interactions and surfaces](smooth-effects.html)
explores more flexible plant-specific curves, while retaining the small number
of biological replicates as a limitation.

A conditional check holds the fitted plant effects and smooth fixed. Quantile
residuals use a fixed standard-normal reference to assess the distribution of
individual scores conditional on those effects; the reference does not preserve
dependence between scores. A marginal check instead draws new plant effects
**and new spline random coefficients** with glmmTMB's simulator. It therefore
checks a broader distribution than that of new plants around a fixed shared
concentration curve. The same scope applies to marginal posterior predictive
checks. Conditional posterior predictive checks draw uncertainty in
fitted coefficients and effects together. These answer different questions;
see [Choosing diagnostic references](model-checking.html). Partial-residual
overlays are not supported for glmmTMB smooth plots. For supported response
families, model parts and current limitations, consult `?"glmmTMB-methods"`.
Multiple linear predictors retain model-wide smooth selection and identify
the conditional, zero-inflation or dispersion model in their plot subtitles;
constant dispersion alone does not add these subtitles.

gratia cannot make a smooth type available if glmmTMB cannot fit it. Effects
require the stored smooth and random-effect information; unsupported structures
with several penalties, models that fix or share joint parameters through
`map`, and rank-deficient smooth models give explicit errors. For a GAM that
does not require glmmTMB's additional model components, mgcv offers a broader
range of spline constructions. Changing the smooth construction or removing
random effects changes the model and needs its own justification.
